name: Convert Markdown into a branded PDF with a table of contents using PDFMint

parameters.content:
## Convert Markdown into a branded PDF with a table of contents

**Who it is for**
Anyone holding Markdown — an AI agent's answer, release notes, a knowledge-base page, a report written in an editor — who needs a finished, branded PDF back in the same request. No headless browser to run, no template editor to log into.

**How it works**
1. **Receive the Markdown document** takes a POST with `markdown`, `title` and an optional `author`.
2. **Set your document branding** is the one node you edit: brand name, accent colour, page format, whether a table of contents is added, and an optional watermark such as `DRAFT`.
3. **Check the request is usable** turns an empty payload into a readable 422 before anything is rendered.
4. **Check remaining quota** asks PDFMint how many credits are left. The `usage` operation costs nothing.
5. **Build the cover, contents and body** does all the work in one place: it numbers every `##` and `###` heading, builds a contents list from exactly those numbers so the two cannot drift apart, skips headings inside fenced code blocks, counts the words, estimates the reading time, and assembles a cover block. It also derives the running header and the CSS from your accent colour.
6. **Render the Markdown as PDF** sends the assembled Markdown to PDFMint with your header, page numbers and styling.
7. **Did the render succeed?** decides which answer the caller gets, because the render node is set to continue on failure.
8. **Return the PDF** answers the POST with the file itself; **Return the error as JSON** answers with a status and a reason, so a caller never hangs.

**How to set it up**
- Install the verified community node `n8n-nodes-pdfmint`. It is available on n8n Cloud and self-hosted n8n; Cloud owners and admins can add it from **More from the community** in the nodes panel.
- Create a PDFMint credential with your API key.
- Open **Set your document branding** and put your own brand name, accent colour and page format in it. Nothing else needs editing.

**How to customise it**
- Swap **Return the PDF** for Gmail, Google Drive or S3 if you would rather deliver the file than answer with it.
- Set `draftWatermark` to `DRAFT` while a document is unfinished; leave it empty for the final version.
- Replace the webhook with a Schedule Trigger to turn a nightly report into a PDF.

*Disclosure: I build PDFMint, and I wrote this template.*

### 1. The request comes in
POST the document as JSON. Required: `markdown` and `title`. Optional: `author`. Any tool that can send an HTTP request can use this — including an AI agent that has just written the Markdown.

### 2. Edit this node, not the others
Brand name, accent colour, page format, whether a contents list is added, and an optional watermark. Every other node reads its settings from here.

### 3. Refuse an empty request early
No Markdown or no title means no document is worth rendering. The caller gets a readable reason instead of a one-line PDF.

### 4. Look before you spend
PDFMint's `usage` operation costs no credits and reports how many are left. Running out is answered with an explanation rather than a failed render.

### 5. Everything is computed here
Headings are numbered, the contents list is built from those same numbers, headings inside fenced code blocks are left alone, words and reading time are counted, and the header and CSS are derived from your accent colour.

### 6. Markdown in, PDF out
One node. The header, page numbers, watermark and stylesheet all come from the config node, so the same workflow renders every document in your house style.

### 7. Did a PDF actually come back?
The render node continues on failure, so an unreachable API arrives here as data instead of stopping the workflow. This node decides which of the two answers the caller gets.

### 8. The caller always gets an answer
On success the POST is answered with the PDF; on failure with a status (422 for a bad request, 500 when the render itself fails) and the reason. The request never hangs.

body.title: Field gateway firmware release runbook
body.author: Platform Operations
body.markdown:
Every deployment to the field gateway fleet follows the same three stages. This
document is the reference the on-call engineer reads before starting one.

## Preparing a release

A release is prepared on the build host, never on a gateway. The build host is the
only machine with the signing key, and the key never leaves it.

### Version numbering

Firmware versions are `MAJOR.MINOR.PATCH`. A patch release may only change
behaviour that is already covered by a regression test.

### Signing the image

The signing step is scripted so the key is never typed by hand:

```bash
# build the image and sign it in one step
./tools/build.sh --target gateway-v3 --sign
```

The `#` above is a shell comment, not a heading, and a document that turns it into
one has already gone wrong.

## Rolling out

Rollouts are staged. Each stage must sit for the full soak time before the next one
begins, whatever the dashboard says.

### The stages

| Stage | Gateways | Soak time |
| --- | ---: | ---: |
| Canary | 3 | 24 hours |
| Region | 40 | 72 hours |
| Fleet | 612 | — |

### Aborting

> Any engineer may abort a rollout without asking. Explaining afterwards is
> cheaper than a fleet-wide regression.

## Rolling back

A rollback restores the previous image from the gateway's B partition. It does not
need the build host and does not need network access to the fleet controller.

### What a rollback cannot fix

Configuration written by the new firmware stays written. If a release changes the
configuration schema, the rollback plan has to name the migration that reverses it.
